name: ZMA

lead: ZMA is a bundle of zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6, created by BALCO founder Victor Conte and sold to athletes as a pre-bed supplement. Bodybuilders take it hoping for better sleep and higher testosterone, which they tie to overnight recovery and more muscle from training.

The claimed chain is that these minerals support sleep and anabolic hormone processes, with timing before bed meant to aid absorption. A 1998 company-funded study reported strength gains in football players, while later studies, including an industry-funded one, found no significant hormone or performance effects.

paras: People take it as capsules on an empty stomach at night, usually as part of a general lifting and sleep routine. Users commonly judge it over several weeks by sleep quality and how recovered they feel. Some variants add 5-HTP.

Sold as a dietary supplement. Variants that add 5-HTP can raise serotonin, which matters if combined with serotonin-raising drugs. Published safety data are not extensively covered in the sources reviewed.

chain: Zinc and magnesium for sleep and T
angle.text: Bodybuilders take ZMA at night for better sleep and higher testosterone, which they link to recovery and muscle gain. The few studies on those outcomes in trained athletes give conflicting results.

lead: ZMA is a night-time supplement that combines zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6, taken before bed by lifters, bodybuilders and other athletes. People use it to support deeper sleep and recovery and to keep testosterone-related processes running normally, with the aim of training harder, recovering between sessions and building more muscle over time. The standard formulation contains zinc monomethionine aspartate, magnesium aspartate and pyridoxine (vitamin B6), and it was developed by Victor Conte, founder of BALCO Laboratories [1][2].

The appearance chain people describe is sleep and recovery, then more consistent training, then a more muscular physique. Zinc is needed for testosterone production, and zinc deficiency is associated with reduced circulating testosterone [3]; magnesium and zinc are also proposed to support sleep through GABA-related signalling [4][5]. Vitamin B6 is a coenzyme in more than 140 enzyme reactions, including the making of neurotransmitters such as serotonin and GABA [6].

Published human studies are few and small. A study by Brilla and Conte in college football players reported greater strength and hormone changes with ZMA, and later independent trials looked at training adaptations, testosterone and sleep [1][7]. A 2004 eight-week trial in 42 resistance-trained men found no significant differences in hormones, body composition or strength between ZMA and placebo [7]; a 2009 trial in 14 men found raised serum and urinary zinc but no significant change in testosterone [8]; and two 2024 crossover trials examined sleep and next-morning performance [9][10][4][5].

On T Nation, members describe ZMA mostly as a sleep aid, with several reporting that they fall asleep more easily or sleep more deeply, and some noting they cannot tell whether it helps [11][12][13][14].

paras: The original product pairs 30 mg zinc, 450 mg magnesium and 10.5 mg vitamin B6 per serving, and the manufacturer advises taking it on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before bed, avoiding calcium because of claimed absorption interference [1]. The same three-ingredient formula was used in the 2024 trials, delivered as three capsules [4][5].

SNAC holds the trademark but the formula is not patented, so other brands sell similar products [1]. A commercial ZMA product, Z-Mass PM, was the product tested in the 2004 trial [7]. Variants include ZMA-5, which adds 5-HTP and is sold as a sleep aid; Wikipedia notes 5-HTP can raise serotonin, which may affect sleep, appetite and body temperature [1].

ZMA was developed by Victor Conte, who founded the Bay Area Laboratory Co-operative (BALCO) in California in the 1980s; Wikipedia's articles give 1983 for the lab and 1984 in the Conte biography [2][15]. BALCO officially offered blood and urine analysis and food supplements, and Conte offered free blood and urine tests to athletes dubbed the BALCO Olympians in 1988 [15]. From 1996 Conte worked with NFL player Bill Romanowski, and the two founded a ZMA-branded track club for marketing [15].

The trademark is held by SNAC Nutrition, and the formula itself is not patented, so many brands sell similar products [1]. The first published study of ZMA was in NCAA football players and was funded by the trademark holder, a fact later commentators noted when discussing the study [1].

BALCO is better known for a separate matter. In September 2003 federal and state agents raided its facilities in an investigation tied to the designer steroid tetrahydrogestrinone, nicknamed the Clear [15]. Conte pleaded guilty on 15 July 2005 to conspiracy to distribute steroids and money laundering, and was sentenced that October to four months in prison followed by four months of house arrest [2][15]. In 2011 he founded the supplement and training company SNAC (Scientific Nutrition for Advanced Conditioning) in San Carlos, California [2]. Wikipedia reports that Conte died in November 2025 [2].
ZMA then became a staple of bodybuilding supplement shelves as an evening product, sold alongside sleep and testosterone-support supplements [1].

The proposed rationale is that zinc and magnesium are involved in sleep and in hormone-related processes, and that athletes who sweat out minerals may fall short of them; taking the combination before bed is meant to support sleep and recovery [4][5]. Authors of the 2024 trials describe the sleep mechanism as proposed involvement of the two minerals in GABA signalling, and note that athletes often sleep less than they have the opportunity to because of training, travel and early or late competition schedules [4][5].

Zinc is needed for testosterone production, and zinc deficiency can reduce circulating testosterone, which is the basis for the testosterone-support claim [3]. Vitamin B6 is included as a cofactor in the formula [1]; it is a coenzyme for making neurotransmitters including serotonin, dopamine and GABA and supports glycogen breakdown [6]. The authors of the 2009 trial and the 2024 trials note that participants were not deficient in zinc or magnesium, which is relevant to who might respond [8][4].

A clinical review distinguishes dietary zinc from pharmacological doses, defined as more than 40 mg of elemental zinc per day, and describes the question of dietary versus pharmacological dosing as debated, including in male hypogonadism [16].

Brilla and Conte reported that ZMA during off-season football training increased zinc and magnesium levels, free testosterone, IGF-1 and strength; Wilborn and colleagues summarise these findings and cite the work as appearing in 2000 in an online exercise journal, whereas Wikipedia describes the study as dating from 1998 [7][1]. It was funded by SNAC Systems, and co-author Victor Conte holds equity in the company [1].

The 2004 trial by Wilborn and colleagues, funded by the manufacturer Cytodyne Technologies though the authors state that they analysed the data independently, was a double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 42 resistance-trained men with a mean age of 27 [7]. Participants took a commercial ZMA product or a dextrose placebo 30 to 60 minutes before bed during eight weeks of a standardised four-day-per-week resistance programme, with testing at weeks 0, 4 and 8 [7]. Serum zinc rose 11 to 17 percent in the ZMA group but the change was not statistically significant, and there were no significant between-group differences in anabolic or catabolic hormones, body composition, one-repetition-max strength, muscular endurance or Wingate anaerobic power [7]. Hormone and mineral analyses used a subset of 26 men because some frozen samples were lost, and the authors note the population was experienced, zinc-replete male lifters [7].

A 2009 study in 14 healthy, regularly exercising men aged 22 to 33 gave ZMA and measured testosterone. Serum zinc and urinary zinc excretion rose, as did urinary pH and urine flow, while serum total and free testosterone and urinary testosterone metabolites did not change significantly; baseline zinc intake from food ranged from about 12 to 23 mg per day, so participants were not zinc deficient, and the authors concluded the finding applied to men eating a zinc-sufficient diet [8].

Two 2024 trials in Nutrients examined sleep. Edwards and colleagues tested ZMA, a maltodextrin placebo and no pill in 19 recreationally trained men, with two nights of prescribed 22:30 to 06:30 sleep per condition, actigraphy and questionnaires for sleep, and testing at 07:00 of countermovement jumps, repeated sprints and a Stroop test [9][4]. There were no significant differences in any sleep measure, sprint result or Stroop result; jump height was lower with placebo than with either ZMA or no pill, which the authors read as a negative placebo effect rather than a benefit of ZMA [4]. Baseline zinc, magnesium and B6 intakes were adequate in the group [4].

Gallagher and colleagues used a randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover design in 16 trained men aged about 22, comparing ZMA, placebo and no pill after two nights restricted to about 4 hours of sleep [10][5]. They measured bench press and back squat at 40, 60 and 80 percent of one-repetition maximum with a linear encoder, grip strength, mood, sleepiness and a Stroop test at 07:00 [5]. There were no condition effects on actigraphy-measured sleep, lifting, grip strength, mood or alertness, and the authors concluded ZMA did not improve sleep, morning strength or cognition in these non-deficient athletes [5]. Both trials list limitations: small male-only samples, actigraphy rather than polysomnography, and only two nights of supplementation [4][5]. Neither tested long-term muscle growth.

ZMA is sold as a dietary supplement [1]. Wikipedia notes that consumption of excess zinc may cause ataxia, lethargy and copper deficiency [17]. The US recommended dietary allowance for zinc is 11 mg per day for adult men [3]. The Edwards and Gallagher trials used a formula supplying 30 mg of zinc, 450 mg of magnesium and 10.5 mg of vitamin B6 per serving [4][5].

For vitamin B6, the US upper limit for adults is 100 mg per day and the EU's 2023 limit is 12 mg per day; toxicity has been documented only from supplements and takes the form of sensory neuropathy, typically at doses above 1,000 mg per day according to Wikipedia [6]. The Edwards authors also note that high doses of B6 may impair sleep [4]. The ZMA-5 variant adds 5-HTP, which can raise serotonin [1]. Product labels and health professionals are the sources for individual guidance.

ZMA is grouped with sleep and testosterone-support supplements in bodybuilding and ascension discussions. On T Nation, one member said it helped them sleep deeper for years [12], another that they fall asleep easier but sleep for less time [13], and another that they had never noticed anything from supplements, ZMA included [18]. A member discussing testosterone said ZMA may raise levels in people who are deficient but does not push testosterone far above normal [19]. Another member who restarted ZMA together with ashwagandha said progress coincided with other changes and that they were unsure which mattered [20].

lore.intro: ZMA comes up in T Nation training logs and supplement threads, mainly as a pre-bed sleep aid and occasionally as a testosterone support [11][12][13][19].
